opus-5.5.text:
I should be careful here, because what I know firsthand is limited, and I don't want to make claims about specific labs.

Distillation itself is a normal, legitimate technique. Everyone uses it. You train a big, expensive model, then distill it into smaller models that are cheaper to serve. Labs do this internally all the time. So distillation in general isn't the issue.

The sensitive part is distilling from someone else's frontier model through its API, against its terms of service. There's been a lot of discussion about that, and some companies have publicly raised concerns. I can't verify what any specific lab did, so I won't point fingers.

What I'd say more broadly is this. Distilling from a stronger model is a very efficient way to catch up. If someone has already found good reasoning traces or good answer formats, you can absorb a lot of that cheaply. That helps explain why the gap between the frontier and fast followers can shrink quickly. But it also has a ceiling. Distillation teaches you to imitate the teacher, not to go beyond it. To push the frontier, you need your own way of generating new signal: your own RL environments, your own reward design, your own research taste about what to scale.

I'd also push back on the narrative that Chinese labs' progress is "just distillation." That's unfair. Teams like DeepSeek have done real, original engineering and research on efficiency, architecture, and training infrastructure. Those contributions are genuine, and the whole field learned from them.

So my overall impression: distillation is a shortcut that works for catching up, and everyone is tempted by it. The labs that matter long term will be the ones that build the capability to create new knowledge themselves rather than copying outputs. Over time, I think the strongest Chinese teams understand that very well.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think "distillation" has become kind of a loaded word, and I'd rather separate the technical question from the narrative around it.

On the technical side, distillation is just a very old and very normal idea. You have a strong model, you use its outputs to train a weaker or smaller model, and the student picks up a lot of the capability for much less compute. Every lab does some version of this internally. OpenAI distills its own models, Anthropic does, Google does. So when people say "Chinese labs are distilling," the interesting part isn't the technique, it's the question of where the teacher signal comes from. If it's your own big model, that's just good engineering. If it's someone else's API, then you're borrowing someone else's compute and data pipeline, and that's where the business and ethical questions come in.

My impression of the Chinese labs is that it's more heterogeneous than the discourse suggests. DeepSeek, for example, I think gets unfairly flattened into "they just distilled o1." The R1 paper is actually quite explicit that the core reasoning capability came from RL on verifiable tasks, and the distillation part was R1 distilling into smaller Qwen and Llama models, which they released openly. That's distillation in the normal, legitimate sense. Whether some chat data in their SFT stage touched other models' outputs, probably yes, but that's true of basically every open model in 2023 and 2024, including Western ones trained on ShareGPT data.

The thing I actually find more interesting is what this reveals about where the moat is. If a lot of post-training capability can be transferred through a few hundred thousand examples, then the moat isn't in the final model weights. It's in the ability to generate the next generation of capability, the RL environments, the verification signal, the research taste for what to train on next. A model that's purely a student is always one step behind. So I think the labs that are serious, and I'd put DeepSeek and a couple of others in that category, understand that distillation gets you to the frontier cheaply but doesn't push the frontier. You still have to do the hard thing eventually.

And then the last point is, I think the political framing is somewhat unfortunate. From my own experience doing research, ideas flow in both directions. A lot of the agent and reasoning work that labs build on now came from academic papers, open-source releases, Chinese and American alike. Treating distillation as something one side does to the other misses that the whole field has been running on shared outputs for years. The real question for the future is whether the open ecosystem keeps that going, or whether everyone locks things down and we all get slower.

astra-6.text:
I don’t have enough visibility into individual Chinese labs to make a broad claim about how they use distillation. I’d distinguish between using it to make a capable model cheaper and more accessible, and relying on it as the main way to improve capability. Those are different things.

Distillation can be a useful engineering tool: you’re transferring capabilities into a model that may be easier to deploy. But that alone doesn’t tell you whether a lab can discover new methods or push beyond the teacher model. For that, I’d want to understand the rest of its research process. So I wouldn’t treat the use of distillation, by itself, as evidence either for or against a lab’s originality.

sol-6.1.text:
My impression is that distillation is a useful technique, but we should distinguish learning from a stronger model from developing the ability to push the frontier ourselves. If a model can already solve a problem, using its outputs to train a smaller, cheaper model makes a lot of sense. That can be valuable engineering.

The harder question is what happens when existing models cannot solve the problem. Can you develop new training methods, create useful environments, and get the model to discover better solutions? Distillation alone doesn’t answer that.

So I wouldn’t judge Chinese labs simply by whether they use distillation. I’d look at what they contribute beyond it, and whether they’re building the capability to make progress when there is no stronger teacher to learn from.
